sentences.text: The species Edmontosaurus annectens reached lengths of up to 12 meters and an average weight of 5.6 metric tons.
Edmontosaurus was one of the largest duck-billed dinosaurs to ever exist.
The skull was roughly triangular in profile and lacked a bony cranial crest.
The brain cavity of Edmontosaurus occupied about a quarter of the skull length and held endocasts ranging from 374 ml to 450 ml.
Exceptionally large specimens of Edmontosaurus annectens measured approximately 15 meters in length and weighed around 15.9 metric tons.
In 2003, researchers described evidence of various tumors, including hemangiomas and metastatic cancer, in Edmontosaurus bones.
The Lance Formation preserves two Edmontosaurus "mummies".
In 2025, researchers detected ancient hydroxyproline in an Edmontosaurus fossil, confirming the presence of original dinosaur organic material and refuting contamination hypotheses.
The genus Edmontosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
The first fossils of Edmontosaurus were discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of southern Alberta.
The specimens for the synonym Claosaurus annectens were collected in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher from the Lance Formation of Wyoming.
Edmontosaurus was a herbivore capable of moving on both two and four legs.
Researchers study Edmontosaurus diet and physiology by analyzing stable isotopes of carbon and oxygen preserved in tooth enamel.
A 2009 study identified four classes of scratches on Edmontosaurus teeth, indicating complex jaw movements during feeding.
Computer modeling from 2007 suggests Edmontosaurus could run at speeds up to 45 km/h.
Computer simulations indicated a maximum simulated speed of 17.3 m/s for a kangaroo-like hopping gait, though researchers considered this unlikely.
Edmontosaurus had slim hands with short fingers, rendering its forelimbs ineffective for swimming propulsion.
Researchers interpreted skull size correlations as strong evidence that Edmontosaurus skull shape changed dramatically during growth.
Edmontosaurus fossils show osteochondrosis, a condition characterized by surficial pits in bones where they articulate.
The Denver specimen, one of two Edmontosaurus fossils under study at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, had a tail top at least 2.9 meters high, a height only reachable by T. rex from the same rock formation.
The genus Edmontosaurus includes synonyms such as Anatosaurus, Anatotitan, Claosaurus annectens, and possibly Ugrunaaluk.
In 1942, Lull and Wright created the genus Anatosaurus to classify several hadrosaurid species that did not fit into existing genera.
Edmontosaurus is currently recognized as having two valid species: E. regalis and E. annectens.
A 2017 study questioned the validity of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus, suggesting it is indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus specimens.
Edmontosaurus fossils date from the Late Cretaceous, spanning the Campanian to the end of the Maastrichtian stages.
Fossils of Edmontosaurus regalis are found in western North America from rocks dating to 73 million years ago.
The Lance Formation, located approximately 100 km north of Fort Laramie in eastern Wyoming, is interpreted as a bayou setting.
The rocks containing Edmontosaurus fossils are older than the rocks containing Claosaurus annectens fossils.
Edmontosaurus annectens differs from E. regalis by possessing a longer, lower, and less robust skull.
There is a debate over whether plant fossils found in an Edmontosaurus specimen represent gut contents or were washed in after death.
